follow_up.question: Can this one-year result be used unchanged for five-year debt?
follow_up.reference: No, a longer maturity changes when principal is repaid and how the upfront fee affects annual yield. Solve the timed cash-flow yield for the longer contract.

instances.text: Consider a manufacturer. One-year debt has face value 450 million dollars, coupon is 12.5 percent, upfront issuance fee is 1 percent of face, and tax is 40 percent. What is the effective annual after-tax cost, as a percentage?
instances.spoken_text: Consider a manufacturer. One-year debt has face value four hundred and fifty million dollars, coupon is twelve point five percent, upfront issuance fee is one percent of face, and tax is forty percent. What is the effective annual after-tax cost, as a percentage?

follow_up.question: What if the fee were deductible immediately?
follow_up.reference: Initial net cash would include the usable upfront tax benefit. That timing differs from a deduction at repayment, so the cash-flow calculation must change.

instances.text: Consider a distributor. One-year debt has face value 300 million dollars, coupon is 13 percent, upfront issuance fee is 3 percent of face, and tax is 20 percent. What is the effective annual after-tax cost, as a percentage?
instances.spoken_text: Consider a distributor. One-year debt has face value three hundred million dollars, coupon is thirteen percent, upfront issuance fee is three percent of face, and tax is twenty percent. What is the effective annual after-tax cost, as a percentage?

follow_up.question: Why is the coupon tax shield smaller than the coupon payment?
follow_up.reference: The shield equals the deductible coupon multiplied by the tax rate. The remaining after-tax coupon is still a cost to the borrower.

instances.text: Consider a publisher. One-year debt has face value 450 million dollars, coupon is 11 percent, upfront issuance fee is 2 percent of face, and tax is 30 percent. What is the effective annual after-tax cost, as a percentage?
instances.spoken_text: Consider a publisher. One-year debt has face value four hundred and fifty million dollars, coupon is eleven percent, upfront issuance fee is two percent of face, and tax is thirty percent. What is the effective annual after-tax cost, as a percentage?

follow_up.question: Why does the upfront fee raise the effective cost?
follow_up.reference: The borrower receives less cash initially but still repays the full face value. The fee therefore increases the cost relative to the usable funding received.
